speaker: Doctor
text: Welcome to the clinic. I'm Dr. Agent, and I see you're having trouble with wrist pain and moving your hand. To get started, can you tell me exactly where the pain is located and if it was caused by a specific injury or if it came on suddenly?

speaker: Patient
text: 34-year-old female. The patient reports experiencing pain in her right thumb and wrist, which radiates to her elbow for the past three months. The pain worsens when she holds her infant son and is alleviated somewhat with an ice pack. She mentions a history of falling on her right outstretched hand about six months ago. She also notes that her mother has a history of chronic joint pain treated with methotrexate. The patient has been taking ibuprofen as needed for her symptoms.

speaker: Doctor
text:
Thank you for the details. Given your mother's history with methotrexate-treated joint pain and your symptoms of pain radiating from the thumb/wrist to the elbow, could you describe the specific nature of your hand movement difficulty, such as whether you have trouble gripping objects or dropping items? Also, have you noticed any visible swelling, deformity, or redness in your right wrist or thumb?

speaker: Doctor
text:
DIAGNOSIS READY: De Quervain's Tenosynovitis (likely exacerbated by repetitive lifting of an infant, with possible post-traumatic contribution from the fall).

The pain localized to the radial wrist/thumb, radiating to the elbow, and worsening with holding an infant is classic for De Quervain's. While your mother's history suggests a genetic predisposition to arthritis, the specific mechanical trigger points towards tendinopathy. Since your X-ray and measurements are normal, I am confident this is a soft tissue injury. I will request images of the wrist to confirm no subtle fractures from your past fall are contributing, but the clinical picture strongly supports this diagnosis.
